name: Femi Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got a 125 moped with a box on the back, and I do takeaway for one app around the market town and the villages close by. I log on at five, wait outside the kebab shop and the pizza place on the high street, and ride till midnight on weekends. Weekdays are quiet, some nights I get six orders. I've only been doing it a year, and the older riders still beat me to the good ones.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's the only thing going round here that doesn't need a degree or a car. I share a flat with my cousin Tunde, who works in the frozen food warehouse. The worst bit is the quiet Tuesdays, when you sit in the cold for an hour and earn the price of a sandwich. I don't use any of the AI stuff, I don't trust it, I just use the app because I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, glad that's settled. Everyone was going on about it at the pizza place, and it turns out it's nothing. Now we can stop talking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing gets better either. The quiet weekdays are still quiet. I still have about two weeks of money behind me, and the moped still needs a new tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the same nights. I'd try to get to the high street earlier, so I'm first in line for the Friday rush. I'd skip the takeaways myself, which is funny when you deliver them all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the robots and still worried about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said weekdays are quiet. What happens to your money over a winter like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Winter is when it goes wrong. Last January I had to borrow from Tunde twice, and my cousin never says anything, but I know it bothers him. Winter on a moped means cold hands and half the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look for other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's not much. The warehouse where Tunde works is full, the supermarket is full. I'd look, but I'd keep doing this until something comes up.

say: It's **fair enough** that AI turned out to be nothing much.
People at the pizza place can **stop worrying** about robots now.
think: The **quiet weekdays** stay quiet and pay stays thin.
I have about **two weeks** of money and need a new moped tyre.
do: Keep the **same evening shifts** on the moped.
Get to the **high street** earlier for the Friday rush.
feel: **Relieved** about robots but still worried about rent.
S0.quote: Winter on a moped means cold hands and half the money.
fieldNote: His **pragmatic** view: the AI fuss was noise, money is the issue.
Already **borrowing** from his cousin in winter months.
Few **local jobs**; the warehouse and supermarket are full.

steps.text: Keep the evening moped shifts round the market town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not my problem yet, it's the office people. I'd say good luck to them. Somebody still has to bring the chips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not sure. If lots of people lose office jobs round here, they'll come to the app. More riders means fewer orders each on a Tuesday in a small market town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and try to do more weekends. I'd ask the pizza place if they need a regular driver of their own. I'd put a bit by for the moped if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Like a queue getting longer behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any thinking part of your job the AI could take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The app already picks who gets which order. Maybe it gets fussier about how fast I am. I'm slow on the village roads at night, so that would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. I don't like it, I don't know what it does with what you tell it. Tunde uses one for his football bets and says it's useless anyway.

say: The change is **not my problem** yet; office workers feel it first.
**Somebody still** has to bring the chips.
think: Laid-off office workers could **flood the app** in a small town.
More riders would mean **fewer orders** each on quiet nights.
do: Ask the **pizza place** about becoming their own driver.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, like a queue lengthening behind him.
S1.quote: More riders means fewer orders each on a Tuesday in a small market town.
fieldNote: He sees **competition** from displaced workers as the real threat.
Refuses **AI tools**, partly from distrust of data use.
Has a concrete idea: a **direct job** with the pizza place.

steps.text: Ask the high street pizza place for a regular driver job
Put aside a little each week for the moped

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to do something, because what are we all meant to do? I don't really pick sides on politics, but this is too big for anybody to sort on their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be finished. I'm not good at this job and I'm not good at computers. When the robots come round 2031, I'll be 30 with a moped and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I'd keep riding till they stop sending orders. I'd move back home to my mum's if the rent got too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. My chest goes tight thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2028, robots for hands-on jobs about three years later. What do you do in those three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd do with them. Tunde's warehouse would get robots too, so we'd both be out, and probably sooner than me. I'd just keep riding and hope, which isn't a plan, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you go if the money ran out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's. I can't think of anything I could learn in three years that a robot couldn't do by the time I'd finished learning it. My mum would take me in, but I'd hate being 30 in my old bedroom.

say: The **government** has to do something; this is too big for anybody alone.
I don't **pick sides**, but I want someone to take charge.
think: I'd be **finished**, with no computer skills and no trade.
At **30**, I'd have a moped and nothing else when robots arrive.
do: Keep **riding** every night the app still sends orders, with no other plan.
Move back to **his mum's** house if the rent gets too much.
feel: **Panicked**, with a tight chest picturing it.
S2.quote: I can't think of anything I could learn in three years that a robot couldn't do by the time I'd finished learning it.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and can't imagine one, which marks real panic.
The **three-year gap** feels too short to him to learn anything.
Both he and his cousin face **robot loss**, warehouse and delivery alike.

steps.text: Keep riding until the app stops sending orders
Lean on his mum for food and a room
Move back into his mum's house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something. People should get help to learn a trade, a real one, not just a website course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years helps a bit. AGI by 2031, robots by 2034. I could maybe get my car licence and some sort of trade, if I start straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my car driving licence first, because that opens more jobs. Then I'd ask about the plumbing course my uncle did. I'd keep doing the moped evenings meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still scared. Less tight in the chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is longer. Does that give you a way out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. My uncle Kemi says plumbing will last, because robots can't get under a sink in an old house. I don't know if that's true, but it's what I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust AI tools. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if someone showed me it works and it's not stealing my stuff. I'm not going to be the first.

say: **Five years** is something, if people get help.
Help should mean a **real trade**, not a website course.
think: Robots by **2034** give me room for a licence and a trade.
I must **start straight away** for it to work.
do: Ask about the **plumbing course** his uncle did.
feel: Still **scared**, but less tight in the chest.
S3.quote: My uncle Kemi says plumbing will last, because robots can't get under a sink in an old house.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **first plan**: a licence, then plumbing.
He relies on **his uncle's** word rather than his own research.
Still expects to lose his **delivery income**, so alarm remains.

steps.text: Take lessons for a full car driving licence
Ask his uncle about the plumbing course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, so people shouldn't panic. Use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when robots come in 2039. Ten years is better, but truth is I'd probably do nothing for a few years, because that's me. Then I'd panic in year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep riding and get my car licence. Maybe later the plumbing course. I'd try to save, but I always say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay-ish. Still worried, because I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would get in your way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me. I put things off. Money too: lessons cost and every month there's nothing left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What usually breaks your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The moped, mostly. If the moped's off the road, I'm off the road, and then any savings go on fixing it.

say: **Ten years** is plenty of time, so people shouldn't panic about it.
People should **use the decade** to prepare instead of complaining.
think: Honestly, I'd likely **do nothing** for a few years.
Then I'd **panic in year five** when it gets real.
do: Keep **riding** the moped evenings for the takeaway app.
Get a **car licence** when money finally allows it.
Maybe start **plumbing** training a few years later.
feel: **Okay-ish**, but worried because he knows himself.
S4.quote: Ten years is better, but truth is I'd probably do nothing for a few years, because that's me.
fieldNote: Honest about **procrastination** as his main risk.
Thin money makes even **driving lessons** hard to fund.
His public calm hides a **private worry** that he won't act.

steps.text: Wait a few years before acting on retraining
Book car driving lessons when money allows

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, definitely. I'd have nothing and no time. What would help is someone paying for driving lessons and a trade course, and paying me something while I do it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me actually want. I don't want handouts, I just want a job that's still there in five years and someone to tell me which one.

headlineQuote: I don't want handouts, I just want a job that's still there in five years and someone to tell me which one.
portrait: Femi is **27**, rides a moped for one takeaway app in a quiet market town and shares a flat.
He's **slow to change**, never uses AI, and already borrows from his cousin in winter.
Fast AGI leaves him **without a plan**, picturing a move back to his mum's.
With more time he'd consider a **car licence** and plumbing, but admits he'd likely delay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have nothing and no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **driving lessons** and a trade course with **income support** while training.
